chapter.title: What is left: the owners' share

cards.body:
Equity is **the part of the house that is yours**. Picture the deed on the kitchen table: you paid a 60,000 deposit on day one, and every mortgage payment since has moved a little more of the house from the bank's column into yours.

Borrow extra against the house for a new kitchen and your share shrinks again. Same photo, same house, thinner slice.
cards.simpler:
Think of owning a house with a mortgage. Equity is **the part of the house that is yours**. You paid a 60,000 deposit on day one. Every mortgage payment since then moves a little more of the house from the bank's side to your side.

If you borrow more against the house, say for a new kitchen, your share shrinks again. Same house, same photo, but a thinner slice belongs to you.

cards.prompt: Maya bought a flat for 300,000 with a 60,000 deposit and a 240,000 mortgage. Three years on she has paid 30,000 off the mortgage and the flat's price has not moved. On a balance sheet, Maya's share today is:

options.text: 90,000, the deposit plus what she has paid off

whyNot.a: That's only the day-one money, not the share today: every mortgage payment since has added to Maya's slice.
whyNot.c: That's the asset, not the owner's share: 210,000 of the flat still belongs to the bank.

cards.reteach: Her share is what she owns minus what she owes. Flat 300,000, mortgage now 210,000, so 90,000 is hers. The deposit started the slice; the repayments grew it.

cards.title: Two ways money becomes yours
cards.body:
Equity on a company's sheet comes from **two sources only**. The first is *share capital*: money the owners paid in when they bought their shares, like Maya's deposit. The second is *retained earnings*: profit the company made and chose to keep rather than hand out.

Each year the company makes a choice. Profit can go out to owners as a *dividend*, a cash payout per share, or it can stay inside the business. Only the kept part lands in retained earnings.

So the recipe is: money put in, plus profit kept, minus losses, minus dividends paid out.
cards.simpler:
A company's equity comes from **two sources only**. The first is share capital: money the owners paid in when they bought their shares, like a house deposit. The second is retained earnings: profit the company made and chose to keep.

Each year, profit can either go out to owners as a dividend, a cash payout per share, or stay inside. Only the kept part becomes retained earnings. So equity is money put in, plus profit kept, minus losses and dividends.

cards.title: Where is the 90,000?
cards.body:
Rosa and her brother Tomas started a bakery with 50,000 of their own money. Year one made a 20,000 profit and they kept all of it. Year two made 30,000 and they paid themselves a 10,000 dividend.

Equity: 50,000 + 20,000 + 30,000 - 10,000 = 90,000.

Tomas looked at the sheet and asked where the 90,000 was kept. Nowhere. It is not a pile of cash in a drawer. It is a label for **the slice of the ovens, the flour and the bank account that is theirs** once the suppliers and the bank are paid.
cards.simpler:
Rosa and her brother Tomas started a bakery with 50,000 of their own money. Year one made 20,000 profit, all kept. Year two made 30,000, and they paid themselves a 10,000 dividend.

Equity: 50,000 + 20,000 + 30,000 - 10,000 = 90,000.

Tomas asked where the 90,000 was kept. Nowhere. It is not cash in a drawer. It is a label for **the slice of the ovens, the flour and the bank account that is theirs** once the suppliers and the bank are paid.

cards.prompt: Pinecone Ltd shows share capital of 100,000 and retained earnings of 40,000. This year it lost 60,000 and paid no dividend. What is its equity now?

whyNot.b: That's last year's equity, not this year's: the 60,000 loss still has to come off.
whyNot.c: That's the loss taken off share capital alone: equity is both lines added together, 140,000, and the loss comes off that total.

cards.reteach: Add the two sources first: 100,000 put in plus 40,000 kept is 140,000. A loss is the opposite of kept profit, so take it off: 140,000 minus 60,000 leaves 80,000. The owners' slice got thinner.

cards.title: It can shrink, and it is not a price
cards.body:
Losses eat retained earnings. Lose more than you ever kept and they start eating the share capital too. Keep going and equity turns **negative: the company owes more than it owns**, like a house worth less than its mortgage. That is a warning sign, not a typo.

To see whether profits were kept or paid out, compare retained earnings this year with last year. If profit was 30,000 but retained earnings grew by only 5,000, about 25,000 went out as dividends.

Equity is a sum of the past at purchase prices, not what a buyer would pay today. A brand the company built itself is not even on the sheet.
cards.simpler:
Losses eat retained earnings first, then share capital. Keep losing and equity turns **negative: the company owes more than it owns**, like a house worth less than its mortgage. That is a warning sign.

To see if profit was kept, compare retained earnings with last year. Profit of 30,000 but growth of only 5,000 means about 25,000 went out as dividends.

Equity adds up the past at purchase prices, not today's value. A self-built brand is not even on the sheet.

cards.body:
Dev opens a report, sees total equity of 2 million, and tells his friend the company is worth 2 million. His friend asks if that means the owners could take 2 million out tomorrow. Dev goes quiet.

Spot it by asking: is this a price or a leftover? Equity is **the leftover from the past**, sitting in ovens and stock and bank balances. A price is what someone pays today, and it lives nowhere on this sheet.
cards.simpler:

Spot this mistake by asking: is this a price or a leftover? Equity is **the leftover from the past**. It sits in ovens, stock and bank balances. A price is what someone pays today, and it is nowhere on this sheet.

cards.prompt: Your cousin asks what the 'total equity' line on a balance sheet actually means. Which answer is right?

options.text: The cash the owners could pull out tomorrow
What the owners put in plus profit kept, minus losses and dividends paid
The price a buyer would pay for the whole company today

whyNot.a: That's cash, not equity: cash is one asset line near the top, while equity is a leftover spread across everything the company owns.
whyNot.c: That's market value, not equity: the sheet records what went in and what was kept, at the prices things were bought for.

cards.reteach: Think of Maya's flat. Her share is deposit plus repayments, not the cash in her wallet and not what an estate agent would quote. Equity is the same: put in, plus kept, minus lost and paid out.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Equity is what the owners put in plus every profit they kept, minus losses and dividends, and it can shrink to nothing or below. It is **a leftover from the past, not a price**, so never read it as what the company is worth or has in the bank.
cards.simpler: Equity is what the owners put in, plus every profit they kept, minus losses and dividends. It can shrink to nothing or even below zero. It is **a leftover from the past, not a price**. So never read it as what the company is worth, or as money sitting in the bank.

cards.body: Search 'annual report' plus the name of any listed company. In the balance sheet, find total equity, then the two lines inside it: share capital and retained earnings. Did retained earnings grow since last year?
cards.simpler: Try this. Search for 'annual report' plus the name of any company listed on a stock exchange. Open the balance sheet and find total equity. Inside it, look for the two lines: share capital and retained earnings. Then compare retained earnings with last year's number. **Did retained earnings grow since last year?** If so, the company kept some profit.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain where a company's equity number came from and say whether past profits were kept or paid out.
